Alexander2,3 Abstract In this study, a computerized measure, Interactive Analogical Measure (IAM), was developed and used to assess young children’s ability to reason analogically
The IAM was equipped to provide corrective feedback and the effects of that feedback were tested for experimental and control groups
Children were randomly assigned to the experimental or control group and the IAM was similarly implemented with the exception of the feedback indicators
There were significant differences between the experimental and control groups for overall performance
Data suggested that the effect of immediate, corrective feedback emerged very early during the test and manifested a cumulative effect across the entire test
It seems that an interactive measure provides meaningful problem-solving experience for young children

Keywords analogical reasoning, children, feedback, interactive measure Analogical reasoning enables children to make inferences about relationally similar phenomena across contexts, which enhances young children’s capability for transfer of learning and schema abstraction (Gentner & Markman, 1997; Goswami, 2001)

Through the process of reasoning analogically, young children explore the salient features of a less familiar object, idea, or action (target) and seek to make sense of it by drawing similarities to an object, idea, or action that is more familiar (source)
In so doing, the children’s perceptive abilities may be enhanced and their conceptual understanding of both the target and the source may be augmented
In effect, such relational reasoning allows children to engage in assimilation and accommodation—abilities rudimentary to conceptual development (Piaget, 1952)
Over many decades, the significance of analogical reasoning has been repeatedly documented (e.g., English, 2004; Goswami, 1991)

Specifically, analogical reasoning has been shown to be foundational to language development (Goswami & Mead, 1992), and conceptual change (e.g., Blanchette & Dunbar, 2002), key to scientific learning (e.g., Glynn & Takahashi, 1998), core to knowledge transfer (e.g., Alexander & Murphy, 1999), and a marker of creative and critical thinking (e.g., Alexander & the Disciplined Reading and Learning Research Laboratory, 2012; 1National Taichung University of Education, Taiwan,R.O.C

In recent years, empirical studies have also determined that analogical reasoning is manifest in young children’s free play (Chiu & Tron, 2004) and is a predictor of preschoolers’ learning effectiveness (Abdellatif, Cummings, & Maddux, 2008; Tunteler & Resing, 2007)
However, there is still much to learn about the nature of analogical reasoning in young chil- dren
The assessment issue, in particular, warrants more attention within the empirical research

If researchers are to understand the nature of analogical reasoning in young children, they must by necessity find tasks or measures that validly and reliably bring this way of thinking to the surface
When one is dealing with very young children who may be less verbally facile or whose experiences and associated conceptual knowledge are predictably limited, concerns over assess-ment are paramount

Often, when young children do not understand what is expected from them in a task, they may not solve the task in ways adults expected (Hessels, Vanderlinden, & Rojas, 2011; Shepard, Kagan, & Wurtz, 1998)
Even if young children may understand the goal of a task, they may not be able to retain focus on that goal due to wavering motivation (Garris, Ahlers, & Driskell, 2002)

For this reason, we sought to embed the assessment of analogical reasoning for young chil- dren within a game-like environment that we would circumvent the issues of unclear goals and unmotivating conditions
We equipped this computerized game-like environment by providing these young children with immediate correct/non-correct feedback

Our intention was to empiri-cally examine whether the inclusion of such immediate feedback enhanced these young chil-dren’s analogical reasoning performance by contributing to goal refinement or maintaining motivation

To better understand the configuration of this game-like environment, we first over - view more traditional assessment of analogical reasoning in young children Traditional Assessments In general, studies of analogical reasoning in young children have been broadly concerned with the application of such thinking processes in the solution of problems presented in narrative form or structured as classical analogy problems

In narrative form, children are presented a problem-solution posed as a story (e.g., Goldilocks and the Three Bears, Goswami, 1995) and are expected to use that information in solution of an unfamiliar problem (e.g., determining the relative mag-nitude of temperature)
In classical analogies of the form A:B::C:D, children may be given the source pair (i.e., A:B) and some portion of the corresponding target pair (e.g., C:?)
Children then select the best term from among options that creates relational correspondence between the first and second pairings

In an attempt to reduce the abstractness and enhance the motivation of such classical analogy problems, researchers have sought to use very familiar objects (e.g., piggybanks or trucks, Crisafi & Brown, 1986) or to cast the problem-solving task in a game-playing context (White & Alexander, 1986)
Whether an analogy problem is posed as a story or in the form of A:B::C:?, assessments of analogical reasoning in young children have faced several criticisms

First, there is the repeated concern that the linguistic demands of the narrative forms may well underestimate analogical reasoning capacities in children who are still developing verbal facilities (Goswami & Brown, 1990)
In regard to classic analogies, children may be unfamiliar to the A:B::C:D structures
For this reason, it is difficult enough for the children to identify the within-group relation (i.e., A:B or C:
lower-level relation), let alone the more complex higher-level relation (i.e., A:C; Singer-Freeman, 2005)
Furthermore, taking tests has not been a frequent occurrence in young children’s lives

Therefore, children may not recognize the goals of the assessment or understand what constitutes appropriate actions within this unfamiliar at Bibliothekssystem der Universitaet Giessen on May 31, 2015 jpa.sagepub.com Downloaded from

In addition, during traditional analogical testing, children are not provided with any corrective feedback; neither are they led to understand the purpose of taking the test from answering questions (Singer-Freeman & Bauer, 2008)
Under such circumstances, children who may possess the cognitive abilities and conceptual understand-ing to respond correctly may fail to do so because they do not know the rules of the game
For instance, a traditional test may be unin- teresting to children, who consequently do not fully engage in the assessment task

This is why a number of researchers of analogical reasoning in young children have turned to game-playing situations or enticing narrative problems to spark and maintain interest (Crisafi & Brown, 1986; Goswami, 1995; White & Alexander, 1986)
Yet, finding the right content and structure to cap-ture and maintain young children’s interest throughout assessment remains a serious concern
The Interactive Analogical Measure (IAM): A Computerized Game-Like Alternative To address the aforementioned concerns and benefits of prior analogy assessments, the IAM was devised

Building on the positive features of prior assessments, such as familiar and interesting content, the IAM preserved the advantages of more traditional analogical testing with young children (e.g., well-investigated processing structure)
Two other features of the IAM are espe-cially noteworthy and pertinent to the current investigation
Because of the computer-delivered nature of the assessment, we could provide immediate corrective feedback item-by-item
Second, this computerization allowed for the inclusion of tracking tools (e.g., eye tracking) that are not possible for paper-and-pencil measures

Within the field of analogical research (Cheshire, Ball, & Lewis, 2005; Siegler & Svetina, 2002) and the general educational literature (Hattie, 2008), there is evidence that feedback is one of the most powerful factors to enhance learner performances

It has been argued that feedback provided by the experimenter enhances performance by maintaining the task goal in reasoners’ working memory (Marcovitch, Boseovski, & Knapp, 2007) and by facilitating the creation of task-based mental models relevant to successful performance (Cheshire et al., 2005)

With the guidance of task-based mental models, young children may apply more top-down control to selectively concentrate on relevant information, while ignoring trivial information (Kirkham & Diamond, 2003), and inhibit dominant impulse behavior to make a reasoned response (Diamond & Taylor, 1996)

The Current Study Overall, based on the extant literature dealing with psychoeducational assessment, especially among young populations, we can hypothesize that the presence of immediate corrective feed-back incorporated within a cognitive task, such as the IAM, could afford certain opportunities for the child and for the researcher
For the child, the inclusion of immediate corrective feedback could serve as relevant information as to the nature of the task, and, potentially, the attributes of a “correct” response to that task

For the researcher, the systematic inclusion of immediate feed-back within an experimental study could provide an opportunity to investigate the effects of such task information on performance—not only overall but also as it unfolds across the task

In effect, even if there is sufficient analogy-specific and general literature to hypothesize that feedback should contribute to significantly better analogy performance among experimental (with feedback) versus control (without feedback) participants, the literature is less clear on the response patterns that may contribute to that omnibus effect

For one, it is not clear whether the influence from feedback would be immediate, manifesting in the first few items of the IAM, or at Bibliothekssystem der Universitaet Giessen on May 31, 2015 jpa.sagepub.com Downloaded from

If, on the one hand, feed- back contributes to more immediate understanding of goals of the problem-solving task (Hessels et al., 2011; Shepard et al., 1998), then we would expect to see changes in performance within the first few items of the interactive measures

On the other hand, if the benefits accrued from feed-back take time to develop (if they prove beneficial at all), then it is conceivable that changes in performance would not be evidenced until later in the analogy task

In fact, this latter perfor - mance pattern is what was reported in several studies of analogical reasoning among children where feedback was provided orally by the experimenters (Cheshire et al., 2005; Siegler & Svetina, 2002)

Thus, given the importance of analogical reasoning to conceptual development, the lingering issues in the assessment of such processes in young children, and the potential effects of provid-ing immediate and informative feedback to analogical performance, we designed the current investigation

Specifically, we designed an experimental study to address the following research questions: • •Is there a difference in performance accuracy on the IAM between those children given immediate, corrective feedback and those receiving no feedback
• •Is the effect for feedback immediately and consistently evident in children’s performance of the IAM or is that effect more apparent in later items of the analogy task

This study may help researchers and practitioners understand (a) how young children approach classic psychoeducational, analogical reasoning tasks, as well as (b) how feedback is reflected in children’s performance, and correspondingly, assessments of their analogical reasoning abilities
Our findings may be useful for researchers who seek to design psychometrically sound psycho-educational assessment tools for young children
Method Participants The participants for this research came from four daycare centers located in an urban city of central Taiwan
Parental permission was obtained for 80 of the 5-year-olds attending the centers (ages between 5.0 to 5.95 years; mean age = 5.51; SD = 0.30)
The 80 children from 14 classes were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (with feedback) or control group (without feedback) with consideration of their classroom placements and gender
For example, if possible, half of the males and females from the same class were randomly assigned to the experimental group for the reason that cur - riculum could vary among classes
After block randomization, the experimental group had a mean age of 5.46 (SD = 0.30), while the average age of the control group was 5.57 (SD = 0.30)
The groups had comparable numbers of boys (21) and girls (19), and the majority of the children (84%) had experience operating a computer or watching others operate a computer

The content and formatting of the IAM drew on procedures and principles estab - lished in prior studies of analogical reasoning in young children (e.g., Crisafi & Brown, 1986; White & Alexander, 1986)
Items of the IAM were established through expert validation by researchers in assessment and child development and by practitioners in early childhood educa-tion

Based on prior research with young children (e.g., Lindvall & Ibarra, 1979), it was deter-mined that illustrations would function better in item construction than photographic representations at Bibliothekssystem der Universitaet Giessen on May 31, 2015 jpa.sagepub.com Downloaded from
Chiu and Alexander 421 in that they were not only simpler in form than photos but were also more stylized depictions of the object of interest

Once items using illustrations were constructed, they were evaluated by 5 early childhood practitioners who judged whether the objects depicted would be easily identifiable and familiar to 5-year-olds
Based on the feedback received, minor modifications in the drawings were made to produce the final set of IAM items
The IAM was a 30-item multiple-choice test with an additional 3 non-scored practice items, which were displayed in a fixed order
These practice items were used to familiarize the children with the tool

The IAM covered analogical relations pertaining to associations that appear in daily lives, such as food, dwellings, clothing, occupations, transporta-tion, leisure, nature, size, quantity, length, and whole-part
Each conceptual idea was represented by 2 items; for example, items related to dwelling were bird:nest::dog:
As shown in Figure 1, in displaying the items for the IAM, we drew on the format for a link-it game with which the children were familiar
Specifically, for the problem bird: nest::dog:?, the source pairing (A:B; bird:nest) was displayed vertically on the computer screen and linked by means of a line to suggest a conceptual association
On the right hand of the screen, an image (C; dog) was placed toward the top, parallel with the “A” term in the problem

Specifically, there was the correct answer (e.g., doghouse), a response within the same conceptual category (i.e., same; another dog), an object that was in an associated but conceptually distinct category (i.e., associated; cat as animal but not dog), and a more particular object that was within the target conceptual cate-gory (i.e., subcategory; bone as object associated with dog)
The four categories of the answers were designed with reference to the principles proposed by Goswami and Brown (1990) for classical analogical testing in young children
We also placed a bold dark line to partition the examples in the previous pair from the question and selection items of the next pair

Overall, the design of the problem and its specific physical layout were intended (a) to visually establish for the children what the components of the given analogy problem were and (b) to spatially distin-guish between the givens and the response options

The computer program of IAM was the same for the experimental and control groups with the exception that no immediate feedback was provided for children in the control group
Specifically when a child in the feedback condition clicked on the correct response option answer, a “○” appeared on the screen accompanied with a “clapping hand” sound effect (Figure 1a)

Conversely, when the child clicked on any of the other three distractors (i.e., same category, associated category, or subcategory), an “X” appeared on the screen followed by a beeping sound (Figure 1b)
These indicators “○” and “X” are well known in Chinese culture representing correct and incorrect answers
No such indicators appeared on the screen when children in the control group clicked on any of the response options—correct or otherwise
We used the Kuder-Richardson reliability index to measure the consis- tency of the children’s answers on the IAM
For this analysis, we examined the responses for sixty 4.42- to 7.42-year-olds, comparable in background to the study sample
Results showed that the children’s answers for the 30 items had high degree of internal consistency (KR 20 = .90; all with feedback)
The accuracy rates of the 4-, 5-, 6-, and 7-year-olds were .32, .52, .67, and 81, respectively
We also looked at the test-retest validity of the IAM by administering and re-admin-istering the test to 18 children after 2-week delay
It was our assumption that some analogical development may have occurred over that time, but the children’s performance remained rela-tively stable, as was the case (r = .67,p < .001)
Procedure In the feedback and non-feedback condition, the tests were similarly implemented with the exception of the feedback indicators
In a set-off space within the daycare center, a researcher met individually with a child
The researcher began by telling the child, “You are invited to play a game

I will tell you how to play, and after that, you will play it by yourself.” Children were told to try “your best, and see whether you can find the correct picture.” We used the practice items to reinforce this procedure with the children before they were presented with the actual test items

For example, in a practice question, the researcher stated that In the drawings on the left side, you can see [body] and [cloth] linked together (researcher points to each of the “A” and “B” pictures)
Please pick one from the four pictures (indicating the four response options) to make a pair with the [head] (pointing to the “C” term), just like the pair at the left-hand side

If the child selected the correct option, the researcher responded, “You are right.” The researcher then explained, “Our body wears clothes just like our head wears hat.” If the child gave an incorrect answer, the researcher responded, “Oops! The correct answer is hat.” The researcher then stated the reason
Following the same procedure, the researcher led the child through three practice questions to familiarize the child with the operation of the test instrument and the goal of the test questions
For each item, the researcher stated, “This is [A], this is [B], and this is [C] (researcher points to each of the “A,” “B,” and “C” pictures), which one is the correct answer

(a finger sweep across the four response options)” The researcher let the child use the mouse to click on the picture she or he wanted to select and refrained from giving any feedback on the accuracy of that choice
In the experimental group, the computer provided instant feedback as to the correctness or incorrectness of each response in the manner indicated earlier
When a child gave an incorrect answer, the research asked whether she or he would like to try again

Data Analyses Kuder-Richardson reliability index was used to measure the consistency of the children’s answers on the IAM
An average accuracy rate of .50 indicated that a given child had responded accu-rately to 15 items of the 30-item measure

To examine the effect of giving immediate feedback, we compared average accuracy rates of the experimental and control groups under the assump-tion that any differences in these rates would be associated with the feedback received by the treatment group

Furthermore, to determine the point at which the effect of giving immediate feedback mani- fests in test performance, we examined performance of the experimental and the control groups for test segments
At the item level, an accuracy rate of .50 indicated that half of the children had responded accurately on that item

However, because performance at item level was expected to fluctuate across the test as a consequence of repeated exposures, we chose to analyze response accuracy for six test segments, consisting of 5 items each
In this way, we could detect any trend in response accuracy in a more reliable manner
We determined the accuracy rate for these test segments by taking the average performance for the 5 items in that segment
For example, an accuracy rate of .80 for a given segment meant that the child identified the correct option for 4 of the 5 items
Results and Discussion Performance of the Experimental and Control Groups Performance consistency
In the current study, the internal consistency for the 5-year-old partici - pants was .80 for the experimental group and .67 for the control group
Based on these data, it appeared that the lack of immediate feedback contributed to less response consistency for the control group across the 30 test items

This finding also supports our hypothesis that under non-feedback condition, children may fail to respond as consistently across the test because they fail to grasp the reasoning required to identify the correct answer and thus may respond more inconsistently

In general, the performance data from the IAM indicated that the 5-year-old children who participated in this study demonstrated the ability to think analogically to a reason- able level on the IAM, whether they received immediate, corrective feedback or not
Specifically, the 80 children displayed an average accuracy rate of .58 (SD = 0.16)

That is, they responded accurately to more than half of the IAM items—a level of performance for all participants well above chance (i.e., between 7 and 8 items for the 30-item measure,t = 9.22,p < .001)
The chil-dren’s performance accuracy for the 30 items ranged from a low of .27 (near chance level) to a high of .93
It seems that there were still some children whose abilities to infer the relational simi-larities between the source and target pairs of the items were not well developed

As shown in Table 1, the children in the experimental group had a significantly higher accuracy rate (M = 0.62, SD = 0.17) for the 30 analogy items than the chil- dren in the control group (M = 0.53, SD = 0.14,t = 2.48,p = .015)
The effect size measured in Cohen’sd was medium to large (d = .55)
That is children given immediate feedback performed much better than those receiving no feedback
The feedback effect reported here may arise both from “hot” and “cold” cognitive mecha- nisms
In the “hot” cognitive aspect, children may be more enthusiastic about solving the ana-logical problems when feedback is given immediately after they respond (Garris et al., 2002)

In the “cold” cognitive aspect, the information conveyed in the feedback may contribute to the understanding of task goal (Hessels et al., 2011; Shepard et al., 1998) and/or facilitate the creat-ing of task-based mental models (Cheshire et al., 2005) that guide subsequent performance
Of course, it is also possible that the performance gains of the experimental group may also come from the children’s successive attempts after they responded incorrectly
However, we found that when the children initially responded incorrectly, their second attempts were often correct (92%), thus, minimizing the practice
As seen in Figure 2, for the 1st 6 items, the performance of the two groups was not very dissimilar
Specifically, the children in the experimental group preformed slightly better for Items 1 and 5 but slightly worse for Items 3 and 6, as compared with the children in the con- trol group
This indicated that the children in the experimental and the control group were reason-ing comparably at the beginning of the test
In Figure 2, the gray area marks the degree of differential performance between the experimental and control groups
As indicated by the dashed line, the differences between experimental and control groups were noticeably greater after the sixth item—a pattern that persisted across most of the remaining items
This pattern suggests that the effect of giving immediate, corrective feedback emerged very early during the test

We suspect that the rapid emergence of the feedback effect comes from the understanding of task goal (Hessels et al., 2011; Shepard et al., 1998); that is, children quickly came to understand what the task required of them and how they were to respond
